analysis.one_liner: Requires annual public reports on whether offshore oil wells and pipelines are being decommissioned on schedule.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress, it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and died there on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to publish a yearly report on offshore oil and gas decommissioning: how many wells, platforms, and pipelines missed their legal cleanup deadlines, how many were approved to be left in place rather than removed, and what enforcement actions the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement has taken. It creates no new rules or penalties — it just makes an existing cleanup record visible to Congress and the public. It was introduced on December 12, 2024, with three weeks left in the congressional session, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing businesses, and taxpayers who ultimately bear the risk and cost when oil companies leave offshore wells unplugged or pipelines unremoved. The annual report would show exactly how many decommissioning applications were required and filed, how many wells blew past their legal deadlines, and whether enforcement agencies followed up, giving the public and Congress the numbers needed to hold operators and regulators accountable.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to report annually on decommissioning applications, wells, platforms, and pipelines that missed the decommissioning deadlines set by federal regulation (30 CFR part 250, subpart Q), and on those approved for decommissioning in place rather than removed.

Requires public disclosure of the status of enforcement actions by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement — notices of noncompliance, orders, citations, civil penalties, and disqualifications from future offshore operations — related to decommissioning.
Requires the report to be posted on the Interior Department's website, making it directly available to the public rather than only to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators, whose missed cleanup deadlines and enforcement records would be published annually. Taxpayers fund the report itself, a minor administrative cost. The bill imposes no new cleanup requirements or penalties, so the direct cost is limited to compliance reporting and the exposure that comes with it.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new deadlines, penalties, or cleanup requirements — it only publishes information that already exists inside the Interior Department, so its real-world effect depends entirely on whether Congress and the public act on what the report shows.
Reporting would begin no later than two years after enactment, delaying the first public report well beyond the point when a supporter might have wanted the data.

The full accounting — counting missed deadlines and listing enforcement outcomes — could impose recurring paperwork on the Interior Department and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement without new funding attached in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost transparency measure: it adds no new mandates but would put a yearly public spotlight on how many offshore wells, platforms, and pipelines have missed their legal decommissioning deadlines and whether regulators penalized anyone. Its weakness is that it relies on visibility rather than enforcement — publishing a tally of missed deadlines changes nothing by itself. As a first step toward accountability for offshore cleanup, though, the cost is trivial and the information is one that coastal residents and taxpayers currently have no easy way to get.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate with only three weeks left in the session, was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and the Congress ended before the committee ever acted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced the Plug Offshore Wells Act on December 12, 2024, for himself along with Sens. Merkley, Wyden, and Markey.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action appears in the record.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, about three weeks after introduction, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
All three cosponsors — Merkley, Wyden, and Markey — are Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators are better off, since the public record of missed decommissioning deadlines and enforcement actions they would have had to face stays unpublished. Regulators also avoid the annual accounting of their enforcement record. No one who wanted more transparency gained anything.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill in the Senate
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Plug Offshore Wells Act on December 12, 2024, requiring annual public reporting on offshore decommissioning.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Ron Wyden, and Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it three cosponsors total, all Democrats.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Joe Manchin (I)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 12, 2024, and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended three weeks later.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape is unknown; what the record shows is that all four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and the bill died in committee without a hearing or a roll call.

industries.note: The bill imposes no new rules, fees, or cleanup requirements, so operators keep doing exactly what they do now. But the annual report would publish how many wells, platforms, and pipelines blew past their legal decommissioning deadlines and what penalties regulators issued — information that currently stays largely out of public view and that could fuel pressure to force cleanup or raise bonding requirements. Offshore decommissioning is enormously expensive and operators have a financial interest in deferring it, which is why public visibility of missed deadlines runs against the industry's interest even when the bill formally changes nothing.
